body:
This issue is for documenting the prints for the T-3_01 SOBOL batch to kick off the testing campaign. For each digital model that is printed, one comment should be made and include the following information. **This is subject to be updated, and a notice will be provided if this is the case to those documenting this information.**

- The .3mf slicer file for the print (should include the supports, and multiple .3mf files should be included if changes were made to the support)
- A picture of each print 
- The 6 letter (a-z and 0-9 allowed) identification for each print
- The measured weight in grams for each print ([scale to use](https://github.com/vertical-cloud-lab/tensegrity-optimization/pull/97#issuecomment-5245151502))
- A note of any noticeable defects for each print
- The [RH%](https://github.com/vertical-cloud-lab/byu-vcl/issues/82#issuecomment-5122007610) for the AMS HT unit (the one housing the TPU) at the time of each print

For each digital model, only one print is needed currently for testing. If the model prints with noticeable defects, additional prints are likely warranted. Each print will have its own unique ID, but only one of these will likely be used for testing and optimization. The following nomenclature should then be used in the comment for distinguishing the "ideal" print:
- official_[UNIQUE_ID] - this is for the "ideal" or chosen print
- [description_of_error]_[UNIQUE_ID] - for the remaining prints
title: T-3_01 Prints

body: During printing of a T3 prism, the H2D produced this error code for the left extruder https://wiki.bambulab.com/en/h2/troubleshooting/hmscode/0300_0900_0002_0001 The extruder appeared jammed and would not extrude filament. The then-current print was cancelled, the filament cleared from both the nozzle and pulled from the extruder, and another print was started. During this print, quality issues began to arise. The first print, during which the error code arose: The finished print, whereas we noticed major print quality issues. Notice the roughness on the struts and the poor quality of the housing unit. Note that the struts were cut relatively in the center for analysis purposes. We ran two small identical prints with both black and white filaments to check the print quality on the left extruder, and found no errors. We then began another print with the same filament and stopped it once it began to show the same errors we were having previously. A top down view of the previous print. Interestingly, the gap-print errors mainly happened in the same directions (i.e. parallel to the same axis). The red lines indicate where these gaps are and the relative direction of where they are. To see if there was a problem with the model, we printed it out of the black filament, and found it to print practically perfectly: We then ran the white filament through again on the same print and found the same errors we had before: The rest of this issue is documenting additional tests to resolve this issue.
title: Diagnosing issue with H2D printing nozzle

body:
**Claude finished @me-madsen's task in 1m 52s** —— [View job](https://github.com/vertical-cloud-lab/tensegrity-optimization/actions/runs/30947327762)

---
### Hypothetical: could you ship `.step` instead of `.stl`/`.3mf`?

- [x] Read the trigger comment (hypothetical — no files produced)
- [x] Check the current geometry toolchain (OpenSCAD kernel, Onshape uploader)
- [x] Answer

**Short answer: yes, but not from the current toolchain — it would require swapping the geometry kernel, and there's a trap where you get a `.step` file that's technically valid and practically useless.**

---

### Why the current pipeline can't do it

Everything I generate comes out of OpenSCAD ([`cad/t3-prism/t3-prism.scad`](https://github.com/vertical-cloud-lab/tensegrity-optimization/blob/32addaf/cad/t3-prism/t3-prism.scad)). OpenSCAD is a **mesh** kernel (CGAL/Manifold) — internally there is no such thing as "a sphere" or "a cylinder," only triangles. `$fn = 48` on line 59 is exactly that: my "spheres" are 48-sided polyhedra. There is no B-rep to write out, so OpenSCAD has no STEP exporter and structurally can't have one. Same for the `.3mf`/`.stl` artifacts downstream — all tessellated.

### Three ways to actually get STEP, in increasing order of effort and usefulness

**A. Tessellated STEP (mesh → B-rep conversion, e.g. FreeCAD `makeShapeFromMesh`).** ~an hour of work, and I'd advise against it. `t3-prism-struts.stl` is **49,846 facets** — you'd get a STEP with ~50k planar triangular faces. It opens in Onshape/SolidWorks, it's a solid, and it is *worse* to edit than the STL: no cylindrical face to grab, no sphere to change the radius of, no edge to fillet. This is the trap — it satisfies "give me a STEP" while satisfying none of the reason you asked.

**B. Port the model to an OCCT-backed parametric kernel (CadQuery or build123d, both Python).** This is the real answer, ~1–2 days. `export_step()` then emits **true analytic geometry**: a sphere is a spherical face with a radius you can type a new number into, a strut is a cylindrical face, fillets are real fillets. Feasibility on our specific model is good — the SCAD uses only 36 `sphere`, 8 `cylinder`, 7 `cube`, and the booleans, all of which map 1:1 onto OCCT and come out *better* than the mesh version. The one genuinely awkward spot is the 10 `hull()` calls (the teardrop joint blend, the accel-mount skirt, the scaffold pillars) — OCCT has no convex-hull operation, so those would need re-expressing as lofts or revolved tangent profiles. Doable, and arguably cleaner geometry than the hulls, but it's the part that makes this a port rather than a translation.

**C. Drive Onshape directly via FeatureScript / the API** so you get a live **feature tree** (sketches, extrudes, parameters) rather than an imported dumb solid. Heaviest by a wide margin. Worth mentioning only because it's the one option that gives you rollback and named dimensions — a STEP import, no matter how clean, arrives in *any* CAD package with no history, so you'd be direct-editing (move face / offset face / delete face / fillet). Much better than mesh, still not the same as parametric.

### Uploading STEP to Onshape

Essentially free — the plumbing already exists. [`cad/t3-prism/onshape_upload_t3prism.py`](https://github.com/vertical-cloud-lab/tensegrity-optimization/blob/32addaf/cad/t3-prism/onshape_upload_t3prism.py) uploads via `/api/v6/blobelements/...` with `translate=true` and polls `/api/v6/translations/{id}`. That same endpoint accepts `.step`/`.stp` with no code change beyond the filename list — and it imports as a **solid Part Studio part** rather than a mesh part, which is the good outcome. The existing mm bounding-box readback check would keep working as-is.

### Three caveats worth having on record

1. **STEP can't replace the `.3mf`.** The `.3mf` files aren't geometry containers — they carry the plate layout, per-part extruder routing (PLA→ext 1, TPU→ext 2), filament profiles, and support settings. STEP is geometry only. It would be an *additional* artifact next to the STL/3MF, not a substitute.
2. **The genuinely editable source today is the `.scad`,** not the mesh — 780 lines, fully parametric, diffable in git. For a change like "make the accel pocket 0.2 mm deeper," editing one parameter and re-rendering is strictly easier than hand-editing a STEP. STEP wins for the different case: someone wants to nudge a face in Onshape/SolidWorks without touching code.
3. **Round-tripping is the thing to decide up front.** If anyone hand-edits a STEP, the SCAD immediately goes stale and my next regeneration silently overwrites their change. Whichever way you'd go, we'd need to pick one source of truth.

**If you ever do pull the trigger:** route B (build123d) plus the existing Onshape uploader, emitting `.step` alongside the current STLs. That keeps generation parametric on my side while giving you real B-rep on yours. Not doing anything now, per your note.

body:
@claude you've been doing a lot of analysis that has more or less been black-box to us, which isn't a terrible thing. We've been spot checking here and there and many of these have been tied to what we saw as reputable standards for analysis and have been backed up independently with Edison queries, etc. However, we'd like to better understand the analysis that you're taking with #86. In particular, it was surprising to me that you went from CFC-180 to suggesting something else (CFC-1080 or something like that?). This got me thinking it would be best for us to spot-check your work. This includes both:
- reviewing the code, including perhaps links to some colab notebooks you create that auto-download specific bits of data (raw download links from this repo on various branches) that are more tutorial in nature and include visualizations, equations, etc., especially backed up by real-sources (cross-checked via Edison)
- providing links to source materials (videos, textbooks, websites, etc.)
 
**Claude finished @sgbaird's task in 30m 28s** —— [View job](https://github.com/vertical-cloud-lab/tensegrity-optimization/actions/runs/30593181458)

> ---
> ### Edison adversarial review — it overturned the recommendation ✅
> 
> - [x] Reuse the existing Edison driver pattern; submit ANALYSIS task [`d9092c5a`](https://github.com/vertical-cloud-lab/tensegrity-optimization/tree/copilot/add-drop-test-protocol-again/edison-trajectories/pu-configs) with all 40 raw CSVs + the series table + our doc + **our analysis script** (so the method itself was auditable)
> - [x] Frame it adversarially — 10 named attack surfaces, "try to break this, not confirm it"
> - [x] Fetch the report + independently verify its decisive claim against the raw CSVs
> - [x] Mark the superseded doc, flag the sibling analyses that share the flaw, commit (`b43fb02`, `b6a296e`)
> 
> Report: [`edison-trajectories/pu-configs/report/adversarial-review.md`](https://github.com/vertical-cloud-lab/tensegrity-optimization/blob/copilot/add-drop-test-protocol-again/edison-trajectories/pu-configs/report/adversarial-review.md) · [per-drop recomputation](https://github.com/vertical-cloud-lab/tensegrity-optimization/blob/copilot/add-drop-test-protocol-again/edison-trajectories/pu-configs/report/independent_per_drop_metrics.csv) · [summary](https://github.com/vertical-cloud-lab/tensegrity-optimization/blob/copilot/add-drop-test-protocol-again/edison-trajectories/pu-configs/report/independent_arrangement_summary.csv) · [trajectory README](https://github.com/vertical-cloud-lab/tensegrity-optimization/blob/copilot/add-drop-test-protocol-again/edison-trajectories/pu-configs/README.md)
> 
> ---
> 
> ### Verdict: **do not select B. "None of these — the sweep cannot decide."**
> 
> Of the four grounds I gave for B: **grounds 2 and 3 fail outright**, **ground 1 does not survive as stated**, and **ground 4 partly survives** as a descriptive warning against A.
> 
> ### The finding that does it — and I verified it myself
> 
> **The 20 ms exports contain ~0.39 ms of real pre-trigger data.** Raw CH5 first crosses its trigger at 0.348–0.390 ms and is only 0.09–2.6 % of peak at `t = 0`. My script's docstring asserts the opposite — *"the record starts on the trigger, so there is no clean pre-trigger window"* — and on that false premise uses a **full-record median** as the baseline, a window that includes the impact and the entire ringdown.
> 
> The "CFC-180 CH5 already reads 22–53 % of its peak at t=0" caveat I wrote is **acausal pre-ringing from zero-phase `filtfilt`**, not truncation. It is not a truncation estimator at all.
> 
> Re-baselining on the pre-trigger window:
> 
> | CFC-180 T | A (1/4) | B (1/2) | C | D |
> |---|--:|--:|--:|--:|
> | published (full-record median) | 1.022 | 0.996 | 0.986 | 0.989 |
> | **pre-trigger baseline** | **1.037** | **1.063** | **1.050** | **1.094** |
> | published T CV | 0.43 % | **0.34 %** | 0.95 % | 0.49 % |
> | **pre-trigger T CV** | **0.54 %** | 1.18 % | 1.22 % | 2.48 % |
> 
> I re-derived this independently in-repo on one drop per arrangement (Signals 1/11/22/32 → T = 1.026 / 1.076 / 1.037 / 1.139) and it matches Edison's per-drop table exactly. The mechanism: the full-record median is displaced by the post-impact ringdown by up to ~15 G on individual tri-axis channels — several percent of these 155–265 G peaks — and it biases the input and the vector-magnitude output differently.
> 
> Three consequences: **no arrangement attenuates** (every T > 1); **A, not B, is the most repeatable CFC-180 arrangement**; and the "T falls monotonically with pulse duration" law in §4 disappears (Spearman ρ = 0.40, **p = 0.60**).
> 
> ### The rest of the teardown
> 
> - **The 450–800 Hz band criterion is an estimator artifact.** My Welch estimate has 305 Hz bin spacing — *one bin in band* — and takes the spectrum of the nonlinear vector magnitude. Under signed-axis linear energy the ordering **reverses**: A 30.7 %, B 7.0 %, C 1.4 %, D 1.5 %; absolute band energy favors A ~20×; input-normalized gives yet another order (D > A ≈ C > B). Ground 3 collapses. Note this is the *second* time this criterion flipped — I used it last round to overturn the spectral-centroid claim, and it was no better founded.
> - **`f·τ ≤ 1.5` is wrong**, and in the direction I guessed. A 5 %-damped SDOF under a half-sine gives maximax/input = 1.64 / 1.54 / **1.28** at `f·τ` = 0.91 / 1.23 / **1.84** — C/D are not quasi-static. Worse for the logic: the SRS peak has near-zero frequency slope, so targeting it maximizes *response* but can *minimize* frequency discrimination — the criterion was pointed at the wrong quantity.
> - **The 519–549 Hz "mode" is unidentified.** CH3 does carry the largest 400–900 Hz output energy in all 40 drops (A 517 ± 6, B 533 ± 3, C 511 ± 37, D 477 ± 54 Hz) — but **CH5, the base, has arrangement-dependent content in the same region**, so forced response, rocking and mount motion aren't excluded. Cheapest resolution: weigh the sensor/wax/specimen, tap-test suspended, repeat with a known added mass at the vertex. Also: the correct mounting standard is **ISO 5348:2021**, not the ISO 5347 our docs have been citing.
> - **Every arrangement-level p-value is invalid.** One fixed-order block per arrangement, lag-1 autocorrelation up to 0.98, several n=10 sequences collapsing toward *one* effective observation. After detrending, T CVs are A/B/C/D = 0.45/0.25/0.70/0.36 % (CFC-180) and 2.03/0.89/0.89/0.84 % (CFC-1000) — A stays worse broadband, but with zero arrangement-level d.o.f. And "C vs D is a null" has 80 % power only for ≳1.1 % in T, so it was never equivalence evidence.
> - **On my own biggest worry — the minimum-variance trap — it agrees and goes further:** no single-specimen statistic can bound an unobserved geometry effect. A has ~20× more absolute structural-band signal; B has lower broadband drift. "That is a trade-off, not a winner."
> - **Peak-ratio T is not an energy-absorption objective.** Ranked replacements: input-conditioned output SRS → band-limited transfer function with coherence → output peak at fixed *measured* incident velocity → ringdown damping → incident/rebound KE loss (the direct metric; needs a photogate/encoder and the moving mass, which still isn't recorded anywhere). Also: **Δv is a processing-dependent descriptor** — agreement with 5.47 m/s free-fall is not validation, and it is not a lower bound as our docs claim.
> 
> ### What to actually do next
> 
> **A 20-drop randomized crossover:** two existing distinct geometries × arrangements A and B, 5 drops per cell, **interleaved in randomized order**, one common trigger level, **≥ 2 ms pre-trigger and 50–100 ms post-impact capture**, with input-conditioned SRS / band-transfer outcomes prespecified before collecting. That directly tests whether B's lower noise pays for its much lower structural-band excitation. It's a screen, not qualification — it can't estimate print variance.
> 
> The two capture-setting changes are worth making regardless: the 20 ms window and the ~0.39 ms pre-trigger are what forced every questionable processing choice here.
> 
> ### One thing that propagates beyond this analysis
> 
> The full-record-median baseline is used by exactly the three scripts that read the new 1.25 MHz / 20 ms exports — `drop_test_pu_configs_analysis.py`, `drop_test_pu_vs_felt_analysis.py`, and **`drop_test_print_defects_analysis.py`**. Every older 125 kHz / 200 ms script already baselines on a pre-trigger window, so those are unaffected. I have **not** re-run the two siblings; the print-defect study matters most because its between-specimen T differences are ~2 %, the same order as the baseline shift, so its "print-to-print scatter is CV 0.72 %" number needs re-checking before it's relied on. Say the word and I'll re-run both on a pre-trigger baseline.

**Claude finished @sgbaird's task in 3m 35s** —— [View job](https://github.com/vertical-cloud-lab/tensegrity-optimization/actions/runs/29932022331)

---
### Durable alternatives to the felt stack ✅

- [x] Gather context (felt-sheet sweep, 201-drop wear findings, pulse/head-room requirements)
- [x] Compile durable-absorber alternatives matched to the rig's requirements
- [x] Write up — new [`docs/drop-test-absorber-alternatives.md`](https://github.com/vertical-cloud-lab/tensegrity-optimization/blob/copilot/add-drop-test-protocol-again/docs/drop-test-absorber-alternatives.md) + cross-links from the felt-sweep and 60 in validation docs — committed and pushed (`5dd76e6`)

---

### TL;DR

**Yes, there are good permanent options — this is a solved problem in the shock-test world.** Commercial drop-shock machines (Lansmont, L.A.B., MTS) hit exactly this pulse regime thousands of times on **polyurethane elastomer "programmer" pads** without replacing them. My pick for this rig: a two-layer permanent stack — **firm PU base + Sorbothane top** (~$60–120 once). Cheapest fix this week: cut pads from a **recycled-rubber horse-stall mat** (~$50 for a decade of spares).

### What a replacement has to reproduce

From the measured campaigns: a ~1.6 ms half-sine input at ~450–475 G CFC-180, with the **raw** CH5 spike held ≤ FS/3 ≈ 3.1 kG. That last one is the discriminating spec — worn felt fails not by changing the filtered input much (446 → 463 G over 100 drops) but by adding high-frequency spike content that eats the raw full-scale margin. So a replacement needs **damping**, not just compliance — which is why pure springs rank low.

### Candidates, ranked

| # | option | life | why / why not |
|--:|---|---|---|
| 1 | **Solid PU elastomer pad** (40–80 Shore A, ½–1 in) | 10³–10⁴⁺ shocks | The industry-standard drop-tower programmer material; pulse very close to felt's; tune via durometer + thickness |
| 2 | **Sorbothane** (¼–½ in, on a firmer base) | ~10⁶ compressions | Very high damping — specifically kills the HF raw spike that's eating CH5 head-room |
| 3 | **Rubber stack / horse-stall mat** | 10³–10⁴⁺ | Cheapest per area; one mat = many identical spare pads |
| 4 | **Silicone sheet** (30–50 A) | 10⁴⁺ | Best compression-set + temperature stability |
| 5 | **PORON 4701 microcellular PU** | 10⁴⁺ | "Felt without the compaction" — engineered anti-compression-set foam |
| 6 | Metal springs (die/Belleville/wave) | infinite | Zero wear but **changes the test**: ~5–10 ms undamped pulse, strong rebound — only if a long-pulse input is ever wanted deliberately |

Avoid: EVA/PE closed-cell foams (compression set — felt's failure mode, faster), cork (crumbles), crushables (single-use by design).

### Before switching the campaign onto it

A stack change re-anchors the input, so the doc includes a qualification protocol: a **mini-sweep** (2–3 thickness/durometer combos × 5 drops, reusing the felt-sheet-sweep template and acceptance limits), a **~25-drop stability check** (elastomers Mullins-soften over the first cycles then flatten — the existing stabilized-OLS scripts verify slope ≈ 0 out of the box), and a **bridging run** with an already-characterized specimen (`prc1kn`/`7xadt6`/`9GMQYQ`, n ≥ 25) so pre/post-switch `T` values stay comparable. Two caveats worth flagging: elastomers stiffen when cold (log lab temp, or lean on `T` to cancel it), and the carriage + plate **mass isn't recorded anywhere in the repo** — weigh it once and any future elastomer/spring sizing becomes calculable instead of trial-and-error.

This is complementary to (not a substitute for) the standing longer-term fix of a higher-range base sensor, and `T = TOP/CH5` keeps cancelling input drift either way.

body:
Issue is operational (coordinating the first crush/drop tests on Jeff Hill's tower) and this repo is the LaTeX MRG proposal with no code or existing test-protocol surface. This PR consolidates the moving parts from the issue thread, adds a literature synthesis, and analyzes the recorded accelerometer data.

### Added
- **`docs/drop-test-protocol.md`** — single source of truth for the drop-test setup, covering:
  - Equipment + links to the TP4 Quick Start / User's Guide PDFs attached on the issue and the training video (https://youtu.be/RNjpAmWWmkQ)
  - The tower is **bungee-assisted** (base accelerates past 1 g): §3.1 reframes the pre-impact specimen lift-off as intrinsic rig physics rather than a setup artifact, and §5 leads with Jeff's first-pass fix (cap how far the specimen's top can rise relative to the base) plus tie-to-base options
  - Quantities of interest tied to the BO objective stack: `g_max`, SEA, full ~10 s ringdown (not just the 200 ms shock), reusability, slow-mo framing from t=0
  - Failure modes from the first instrumented drop: bungee-driven specimen lift-off pre-impact, ~25° cage tilt from loose rod/hole clearance, slow-mo starting after hoist release
  - @sgbaird's three-test next-iteration plan: bare specimen → plate-only (uninstrumented) → instrumented cage drop
  - Mitigations: constrain specimen to base / cap upward travel, tighter rod/plate tolerance (re-drill or thin metal plates, optionally linear bushings), top-plate retention clips, longer-term vertex-mounted accelerometer inside an acrylic cage, independent lab access for all three students
  - Cross-references to companion modalities out of scope for the first drop (high-speed camera, shaker transfer function, slug-firing gas gun, Polytec LDV)

- **`edison-trajectories/drop-test/`** — Edison Scientific LITERATURE_HIGH synthesis (task `653d7d39`) on drop-tower troubleshooting for small 3D-printed lattice/tensegrity specimens: ~57 KB report, full JSON dump, submission record, and README. Idempotent driver at **`scripts/edison/submit_drop_test.py`**. Surfaces a standards stack (ASTM D5276/D7136/D3332, ISO 6603/1683/5347, MIL-STD-810 method 516, SAE J211) and recommendations (linear sleeve bearings, magnetic/elastic top-plate hold-down, ≥10 s ring-buffer DAQ, SAE J211 CFC filtering, n ≥ 5 + CV, ≥5000 fps DIC; closest analogues Pajunen 2019, Dwyer 2023).

- **First drop-test data analysis** of the five TP4 accelerometer exports posted by @me-madsen (`Signal 10–14`, 4-channel, 125 kHz, 0.2 s window):
  - **`data/drop-tests/raw/`** — committed raw export files
  - **`scripts/analysis/drop_test_analysis.py`** — loader, SAE J211 CFC-1000 / CFC-180 filtering, peak/pulse/PSD metrics, and figure generation
  - **`data/drop-tests/figures/`** — full-window CH1 overlay, per-run impact zoom (raw vs filtered), peak-g bar chart, PSD, and CH4 trigger-artifact plot
  - **`docs/drop-test-analysis.md`** + **`data/drop-tests/README.md`** — findings: the "audrey" tensegrity specimen reduces CFC-180 peak acceleration ~74–79 % vs the no-specimen control (~370–463 G vs ~1,792 G), while the PETG run's raw peak is within ~1 % of the control (≈ direct plate-on-plate hit), strong evidence of the bungee-driven lift-off; CH4 carries a fixed ~1.4 kG trigger/release artifact at t≈4.2 ms in every run. Caveats noted: unconfirmed channel map, 200 ms window only, n = 1 for control/PETG, no Δv/SEA quoted yet.

- **Vertex vs. acrylic-plate T3-prism drop-test data and analysis** posted by @ctrhjk (PR #67), under **`data/drop-tests/vertex-acrylic/`**:
  - **`raw/`** — eight TP4 exports `{n0jdwk, m6cyoq, T3_0103, T3_0000}_Signal{1,2}.csv` (`Signal1` = vertex-mounted, `Signal2` = acrylic-plate), single drop per configuration at 13 ft, 200 ms / 125 kHz
  - **`README.md`** — channel map (CH1 removed; CH2–CH4 tri-axis; CH5 single-axis; CH4 = 1000 G trigger) with full-scale/sensitivity per channel, per-specimen file index, and @ctrhjk's observations (clip-height/no-trigger issue, hot-glue z-axis mount limitation, `m6cyoq` strut and `T3_0103` TPU-tendon damage after the acrylic test, and the invalid `T3_0000` acrylic run where the accelerometer fell off)

Caveats: n = 1 per (specimen, mount), 200 ms window only, partial-pulse Δv, unconfirmed CH4/CH5 axis correspondence.

- **Clip-height sweep & base-plate accelerometer-check diagnostic** posted by @ctrhjk, under **`data/drop-tests/clip-height/`** — drilling into why the acrylic-plate configuration repeatedly fails to trigger:
  - **`raw/Accelerometer_check_Signal1.csv`** + **`README.md`** — the one triggered base-plate CSV (tri-axis on the bottom plate, 13 in drop) plus a setup README documenting both experiments: the clip-height sweep (extra bungees cured fly-off; tri-axis on the acrylic plate; clips at 0.5/1/1.5/2 in, two drops each; **0/8 drops triggered**, video only) and the base-plate accelerometer check, with the shared channel map

  - **`docs/drop-test-input-output-analysis.md`** — findings: the input-output design works — **20/20 drops triggered cleanly**, removing the bungees makes the input nearly constant (235–248 G CFC-180, ≤1.7 % CV), and **transmissibility now discriminates geometry** (`yqpmx1` ≈ 0.96 is the only attenuator, `h8Lbev` ≈ 1.09, `practice`/`n0jdwk` ≈ 1.17–1.19), making `T` (or output-peak-at-fixed-input) a usable BO objective; a mild within-run drift across the five cyclic drops is flagged as most likely hot-glue-mount-driven. Idempotent driver **`scripts/edison/submit_input_output.py`** + fetch **`scripts/edison/fetch_input_output.py`**; a cross-ch...

- **Drops-per-specimen variance, sample-size, and timing meta-analysis** answering @me-madsen's question (PR #82 comment 5026945744: minimum drops per specimen, variance so far, and set duration at ~42 s/drop at 60 in), under **`data/drop-tests/sample-size/`** (derived — no raw data of its own):

**Claude finished @me-madsen's task in 40s** —— [View job](https://github.com/vertical-cloud-lab/tensegrity-optimization/actions/runs/29618557171)

---
### Current parameters and constraints for the tensegrity BO campaign

- [x] Read `bo/tensegrity_campaign.py` (source of truth for the campaign design space)
- [x] Summarize parameters, objectives, and constraints

All of the below is defined in [`bo/tensegrity_campaign.py`](https://github.com/vertical-cloud-lab/tensegrity-optimization/blob/834ca15/bo/tensegrity_campaign.py) (`PARAMETERS` at [L117–L219](https://github.com/vertical-cloud-lab/tensegrity-optimization/blob/834ca15/bo/tensegrity_campaign.py#L117-L219), `OBJECTIVES` at [L221–L225](https://github.com/vertical-cloud-lab/tensegrity-optimization/blob/834ca15/bo/tensegrity_campaign.py#L221-L225)). Bounds trace to PR #24's Edison literature table ("Recommended Numeric Bounds", task `5ae24eaf-…`).

#### Continuous (range) parameters — 7

| Parameter | Bounds | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| `strut_diameter_mm` | [1.5, 5.0] mm | PETG strut Ø (Pajunen used ~3 mm) |
| `strut_length_mm` | [15.0, 50.0] mm | H2D-friendly window; with Ø sets slenderness L/D |
| `cable_diameter_mm` | [1.0, 3.0] mm | TPU tendon Ø, printable on 0.4 mm nozzle |
| `twist_angle_deg` | [10°, 45°] | prism / stacked-prism twist |
| `prestress_pct` | [0%, 5%] | tendon prestrain (Pajunen sweet spot ≈ 2%) |
| `petg_infill_pct` | [40%, 100%] | strut infill fraction |
| `interface_wrap_thickness_mm` | [0.4, 2.0] mm | PETG–TPU joint reinforcement (Khatri 2024) |

#### Integer / ordered-choice — 1

| Parameter | Values |
|---|---|
| `struts_per_cell` | {3, 4, 6, 8, 12} (ordered choice) |

#### Categorical (choice) parameters — 5

| Parameter | Values |
|---|---|
| `topology` | truncated_octahedron, simplex_4_strut, t3_prism, stacked_prism |
| `tiling` | 1×1×1, 1×1×2, 2×2×1, 2×2×2, 3×3×2 |
| `tpu_shore` | 85A, 95A (ordered) |
| `petg_infill_pattern` | rectilinear, grid, gyroid |
| `build_orientation` | vertical, horizontal, 45° |

That's a 13-dimensional design space total (7 continuous + 1 integer + 5 categorical).

#### Objectives (multi-objective, qNEHVI via Ax's default strategy)

| Objective | Direction | Threshold (hypervolume reference point) |
|---|---|---|
| `F_peak_N` — peak transmitted force | minimize | 2500 N |
| `SEA_J_per_g` — specific energy absorption | maximize | 0.05 J/g |
| `eta` — compaction efficiency | maximize | 0.20 |

The thresholds are the "worst tolerable" outcomes defining the hypervolume reference point; the comments at [L73–L80](https://github.com/vertical-cloud-lab/tensegrity-optimization/blob/834ca15/bo/tensegrity_campaign.py#L73-L80) note they're placeholders spanning the dummy evaluator's feasible range and should be re-chosen from pilot data.

#### Constraints

**There are currently no parameter constraints or outcome constraints.** The honegumi scaffold `CONFIG` in [`bo/generate_scaffold.py`](https://github.com/vertical-cloud-lab/tensegrity-optimization/blob/834ca15/bo/generate_scaffold.py) has all constraint options (`sum` / `order` / `linear` / `composition`) turned off, and `tensegrity_campaign.py` passes no `parameter_constraints` or `outcome_constraints` to `AxClient.create_experiment`. The only constraint-like machinery in play is the box bounds above plus the three objective thresholds. (A natural future addition would be an order/linear constraint tying `strut_length_mm` to `strut_diameter_mm` to enforce the Edison table's L/D ∈ [8, 25] slenderness window — currently handled only implicitly by the bound choices.)

#### Campaign loop settings

`N_ITERATIONS = 5`, `BATCH_SIZE = 2`, `SEED = 0` ([L58–L62](https://github.com/vertical-cloud-lab/tensegrity-optimization/blob/834ca15/bo/tensegrity_campaign.py#L58-L62)) — Sobol quasi-random initialization followed by model-based MOO acquisition (Ax defaults), evaluated against the analytical `simulate_specimen` dummy until experimental data lands.

Note: per @sgbaird's comment on 2026-06-27, printer processing parameters (e.g., temperatures) are anticipated additions to this design space but are **not yet included**.

---

_Originally posted by @claude[bot] in https://github.com/vertical-cloud-lab/tensegrity-optimization/issues/30#issuecomment-5008175231_

body:
This is the next step in our research of tensegrity structures. Here's a draft of the abstract:

We present an exploration of non-prismatic tensegrity configurations in order to improve the impact absorption capabilities of tensegrity structures. We currently use a hexagon-based, tensegrity-like lattice arrangement and FDM fabrication to create a prototype TPU and PLA structure capable of protecting a payload under high-impact conditions. To improve payload protection for future Mars landers, our goal is to supplement future Mars exploration techniques through impact absorption in a Mars lander using Bayesian optimization of lattice base-unit geometry. The designs are validated using controlled drop testing devices, as well as real-world field demonstrations in which we use high fidelity materials for testing these structures. Structures are dropped from different angles to evaluate their anisotropic properties. The prototype is being optimized for consistent impact absorption regardless of landing orientation. Preliminary experimental results demonstrate successful payload protection across a range of testing conditions and design parameters.
title: Tensegrity-like Lattice Structures Abstract for TMS 2027

[Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code) is an AI coding agent that can help with:

### Important Notes

- **This workflow won't take effect until this PR is merged**
- **@claude mentions won't work until after the merge is complete**
- The workflow runs automatically whenever Claude is mentioned in PR or issue comments
- Claude gets access to the entire PR or issue context including files, diffs, and previous comments

### Security

- Our Anthropic API key is securely stored as a GitHub Actions secret
- Only users with write access to the repository can trigger the workflow
- All Claude runs are stored in the GitHub Actions run history
- Claude's default tools are limited to reading/writing files and interacting with our repo by creating comments, branches, and commits.
- We can add more allowed tools by adding them to the workflow file like:

```
allowed_tools: Bash(npm install),Bash(npm run build),Bash(npm run lint),Bash(npm run test)
```

There's more information in the [Claude Code action repo](https://github.com/anthropics/claude-code-action).

After merging this PR, let's try mentioning @claude in a comment on any PR to get started!

body:
Issue #75 recovers from agent failures on PR #20 by establishing a clean branch for the ASME Journal of Mechanical Design (JMD) manuscript and addressing the outstanding peer-review feedback.

This branch now **merges all commits from PR #20's `copilot/create-manuscript-template`**, bringing in the full `manuscript/` (body, SI, build infrastructure), figures, and Edison scripts. `ISSUE_75_CONTEXT.md` remains as a consolidated working reference for the Issue #19 / PR #20 history.

### Round-2 review feedback addressed (comment 4687197892)

- **Scope**: Title/abstract/intro now consistently frame a planetary-lander/payload energy absorber; the crutch-tip appears only as a future-work item in the Discussion; the abstract uses FDM and omits the crutch-tip motivation.
- **Table 1 ↔ parameterization**: Deferred to the authoritative T3-prism BO code (`bo/t3_prism_sobol_batch.py`, PR #35) — a 5-variable continuous search space (`R`, `H`, twist, a single strut diameter, a single cable diameter) with no categorical variables. Removed the "12→4 orbit axes (1 strut + 3 cable)" claim; Table 1 now matches the code.
- **Tendon diameter**: Made continuous (3.0–5.5 mm) throughout; removed the categorical `{1.2,1.8,2.4,3.0,4.5}` mm set.
- **BO method**: Specified SAASBO (justified for better UQ/predictive accuracy even at ~5 variables), Matérn-5/2 ARD kernel, model-inferred noise, n=9 Sobol initialization followed by T=10 batches × q=5 prints (59 specimens total), fixed-seed policy, and a Zenodo DOI placeholder.
- **Novelty**: Added a comparison table vs Pajunen 2019 / Intrigila 2022 / Mo 2023 (architecture / fabrication / optimization / ground-truth).
- **Language**: Softened "ensure cyclic interface durability" pending pull-out/fatigue data; standardized FFF → FDM throughout.

### Metal-analog validation plan

Added a Methods subsection plus an SI section describing a validation campaign using hollow aluminum rods and stainless-steel threaded cables. Predicted worst-, mediocre-, and best-performing designs (not only the top performers) will be built and compared against their PLA/TPU equivalents to test rank-order preservation, with a placeholder results table, a rank-correlation figure, and image callouts for the assembled/printed structures (true placeholders for now).

### Edison round-3 mock review

Submitted the revised manuscript + SI to Edison ANALYSIS for another round of mock reviewer + editor feedback (task `d17a2155`, committed under `edison-trajectories/mock-jmd-review-3/`). Decision: **Major Revision**, explicitly improved over round 2, with all round-2 items acknowledged resolved; the remaining gate is the intentional placeholder Results/Discussion. Also fixed a budget inconsistency flagged by the reviewers (now n=9 + T=10×q=5 = 59 specimens).

### Round-3 review feedback addressed (comment 4699376594)

Implemented the actionable round-3 items (those not requiring real campaign data):

- **Citations now real (no longer TODO promises)**: Added and wired in the primary SAASBO (Eriksson & Jankowiak 2021) and TuRBO (Eriksson et al. 2019) papers, the canonical energy-absorber-metric references (Gibson & Ashby 1997; Avalle, Belingardi & Montanini 2001; Tan et al. 2005; Michailidis et al. 2011), and the SAE J211/1 impact-instrumentation standard for CFC-180 filtering; removed the matching "cite once added to bib" notes.
- **BO formulation pre-committed**: The primary reported campaign is now stated as a constrained multi-objective problem (maximize SEA and compaction efficiency subject to a peak-force bound fixed from the rigid control), acquisition = qNEHVI, with the hypervolume reference point anchored at the rigid-control point; LogEI single-objective is kept only as a baseline, and the robust/evolution-guided variants are demoted to a contingency.
- **SAASBO justified empirically** by benchmarking against a standard single-task GP baseline with the same Matérn-5/2 ARD kernel.
- **Scope discipline**: The Introduction now explicitly places off-axis/combined loading, multi-hit/cyclic durability, and landing-attitude variability out of scope (future work), and scopes the novelty/generality claims to the single-cell prototype space.
- **Joint diameter**: Added the rationale for fixing `d_j` at 7.0 mm.
- **As-built resolution**: New paragraph noting the nominally continuous `d_s`/`d_t` are discretized by nozzle/line-width/support, with measured diameters reported and dimensional spread folded into the inferred noise.
- **Metal-analog test**: Pre-specified the rank-preservation metric as Spearman ρ_s on SEA (peak force secondary) and reframed it as a stringent exploratory transfer test.

Data-dependent items (Results/Discussion, Table 3 print settings, Zenodo DOI) remain honest placeholders.

### Edison round-4 mock review

Submitted the further-revised manuscript + SI to Edison ANALYSIS for a fourth round of mock reviewer + editor feedback (task `a81649dc`, committed with its notebook artifact under `edison-trajectories/mock-jmd-review-4/`). Decision: **Major Revision**, "closer to publishable form than the prior round-3 Major Revision." The editor explicitly confirms all four round-3 citation gaps are closed (SAASBO, TuRBO, SEA/densification metrics, SAE J211/1) and that the constrained multi-objective formulation, empirical SAASBO framing, consistent budget, justified joint diameter, acknowledged diameter discretization, and pre-specified metal-analog rank criterion are resolved. The remaining gate is the inherent placeholder Results/Discussion; the only new reference ask is to integrate the already-flagged tensegrity-AM works (Bauer 2021, Pajunen 2021 EML, Santos 2023, Sabouni-Zawadzka 2024) once verified.

### Round-4 review feedback addressed (comment 4700329518)

Integrated the already-flagged tensegrity additive-manufacturing literature — the only non-data reference ask remaining from round 4. Each DOI was verified against Crossref before citing, and the prior `\todo{}` placeholder note was replaced with measured prose positioning this work against the printed-tensegrity literature in the multi-material / tensegrity-architecture background. References added to `manuscript/references.bib` and wired into `manuscript-body.tex`:

- Bauer et al. 2021 (*Adv. Mater.* 33(10):2005647, `10.1002/adma.202005647`)
- Pajunen et al. 2021 (*Extreme Mech. Lett.* 44:101236, `10.1016/j.eml.2021.101236`)
- Sabouni-Zawadzka et al. 2024 (*Arch. Civ. Eng.* 70(2):343–357, `10.24425/ace.2024.150987`)
- Almeida et al. 2025 (*Int. J. Solids Struct.* 322:113590, `10.1016/j.ijsolstr.2025.113590`)
- Davami et al. 2025 (*Int. J. Impact Eng.* 198:105208, `10.1016/j.ijimpeng.2024.105208`)
- Wang et al. 2026 (*Addit. Manuf.* 118:105107, `10.1016/j.addma.2026.105107`)

The three "verify-then-cite" extras (Almeida, Davami, Wang) all verified, so they were folded in as the closest dynamic/impact and integrated-fabrication tensegrity-AM works. Santos 2023 (`10.1002/adma.202300639`) was already cited from an earlier round.

### Edison round-5 mock review

Submitted the revised manuscript + SI to Edison ANALYSIS for a fifth round of mock reviewer + editor feedback (task `e4c536b4`, committed with its notebook artifact under `edison-trajectories/mock-jmd-review-5/`). Decision: **Major Revision**, "a meaningful improvement over the round-4 submission … closer to acceptance." The Associate Editor explicitly states the round-4 tensegrity-AM reference ask is now resolved and that all prior bibliographic gaps are closed (SAASBO, TuRBO, SEA/densification metrics, SAE J211/1, plus this tensegrity-AM set), and Reviewer #3 confirms the new references are used appropriately (architecture-class evidence, not proof of the specific PLA/TPU process or internal-anchor joint). The remaining gate is the inherent placeholder Results/Discussion, synthetic example figures, and TBD process/test parameters; the only non-data suggestions are optional/strengthening (justify the homoscedastic inferred-noise choice, rename the novelty table, optionally one more transmitted-force→absorber-design citation).

### Build

Rebuilt all PDFs (manuscript, supplementary, todos, and a latexdiff diff against the pre-session baseline) and recompiled the fabrication-workflow figure. Direct download links for co-author review were posted in the PR comment reply.

body:
The single-axis and tri-axis accelerometers on the bungee-assisted drop tower report different accelerations. This adds a reproducible analysis of the 06/02/2026 TP4 series (table export + 13 time-domain events, 4 channels @ 125 kHz) to explain why, and what to fix. The analysis was reviewed independently by Edison Scientific, and its feedback (impact-windowed peak detection; corrected CH4 interpretation) is folded in. It also adds a follow-up analysis of a second, **co-located** TP4 calibration series (06/08/2026), a third **corrected-sensitivity, metal-mount, height-sweep** series (06/09/2026), and a fourth **five-channel** series (06/10/2026) that adds a properly-ranged single-axis on CH5 and finally closes out the cross-calibration — all posted later in the thread.

## Changes
- **`scripts/analysis/accelerometer_tuning_analysis.py`** — parses TP4 time-domain exports, applies SAE J211 CFC-180/CFC-1000 phaseless filtering, and emits per-event time-series, PSD, a CH1 saturation plot, a CH1-vs-CH4 peak bar chart, a CH1-vs-CH4 impact alignment plot, and `peak_summary.csv`. Filtered peaks are searched inside a **±1 ms window around the CH4 impact** (located in the first ~10 ms), not over the whole 0.2 s record.
- **`data/drop-tests/accelerometer-tuning/`** — the 14 source CSVs under `raw/`, derived `peak_summary.csv` (now including impact time and impact-windowed peaks), and a README documenting format + inferred channel mapping (CH1 = single-axis; CH2–CH4 = tri-axis X/Y/Z).
- **`docs/accelerometer-tuning-analysis.md`** + `docs/figures/accelerometer-tuning/` — findings and troubleshooting.
- **`scripts/edison/submit_accelerometer_tuning.py`** + **`edison-trajectories/accelerometer-tuning/`** — bundles the dataset, analysis script, findings, and figures into one collection, uploads it, and submits an Edison `ANALYSIS` task for independent feedback. Task `015f36e1-0a1c-4aed-a9a3-1d1924983c4a` (status: success) has been **fetched and committed**: the reviewer's answer (`.md`), full response (`.json`), notebook (`.ipynb`), and corrected peak table + alignment figure under `reviewer-artifacts/`.
- **`scripts/analysis/accelerometer_calibration_analysis.py`** + **`data/drop-tests/accelerometer-calibration/`** + **`docs/accelerometer-calibration-analysis.md`** + `docs/figures/accelerometer-calibration/` — analysis of the **co-located** 06/08/2026 "Accelerometer callibaration" series (8 TP4 CSVs: `500G_Signal5` aborted + seven 1000 G drops), where both sensors are on the bottom acrylic plate and the known settings are CH1 = single-axis 20 kG/0.25 mV/G and CH2–CH4 = tri-axis 10 kG/1.0 mV/G. Reuses the CFC-180/CFC-1000 + impact-windowing machinery, runs a zero-intercept CH1-vs-CH4 cross-calibration, flags CH1 full-scale clipping, and emits a co-located overlay, a regression plot, a clipping zoom, a repeatability plot, and `calibration_summary.csv`.
- **`scripts/analysis/accelerometer_calibration2_analysis.py`** + **`data/drop-tests/accelerometer-calibration-2/`** + **`docs/accelerometer-calibration2-analysis.md`** + `docs/figures/accelerometer-calibration-2/` — analysis of the third 06/09/2026 "Accelerometer Callibartion 2" series (15 TP4 CSVs: 10/15/20 in drop heights × 5 reps; 5 in didn't trigger). Here the per-channel sensitivities were re-entered from the calibration certificates (CH1 0.25 → 11.61 mV/G; CH2 1.0 → 0.690; CH3 → 0.667; CH4 → 0.734 mV/G) and both sensors were moved off the acrylic plates onto the bare metal load, ~1/4 in apart. Reuses the CFC-180/CFC-1000 + impact-windowing machinery, tracks the per-height amplitude sweep, runs a zero-intercept CH1-vs-CH4 fit, flags CH1 full-scale clipping, and emits an overlay, a clipping zoom, an amplitude-sweep plot, a regression plot, and `calibration_summary.csv`.
- **`scripts/analysis/accelerometer_calibration3_analysis.py`** + **`data/drop-tests/accelerometer-calibration-3/`** + **`docs/accelerometer-calibration3-analysis.md`** + `docs/figures/accelerometer-calibration-3/` — analysis of the fourth 06/10/2026 "AC3" series (15 **five-channel** TP4 CSVs: 10/15/20 in × 5 reps; 5 in didn't trigger). A second, much lower-sensitivity single-axis accelerometer was added on **CH5** (1.059 mV/G → 9442.9 G range), placed on the very left; CH1 and CH2–CH4 were unmoved and all channels were moved to the 10 V range, with CH4 the only trigger source. The script adds a 5-channel TP4 loader (reusing the CFC-180/CFC-1000 + impact-windowing machinery, CH4 still the impact axis), runs a primary zero-intercept **CH5-vs-CH4** cross-calibration plus a clip-limited CH1-vs-CH4 fit, tracks the per-height amplitude sweep, records the CH4↔CH5 peak-time lag, flags per-channel clipping, and emits a CH4-vs-CH5 overlay, a CH1-vs-CH5 clipping comparison, an amplitude-sweep plot, a regression plot, and `calibration_summary.csv`.

## Findings (06/02/2026 tuning series)
- **CH1 (single-axis) saturates** at a recurring ~8806 G ceiling (events 2/3/5). This is **analog** full-scale saturation (a smooth ~180 µs compressed top), not a hard digital ADC clip — its peak is invalid there, so it cannot be matched against the unsaturated tri-axis.
- **Raw peaks are mount-resonance ringing** (PSD energy past 20 kHz); CFC filtering is required before any comparison (e.g. event 1 CH1 at impact: 2576 G raw → 333 G CFC-180).
- **CH4's recurring ~4.2 ms peak is the real mechanical impact, not a trigger/magnet artifact** — it is <0.5 G in the aborted drops (events 6–8) and has a ~280 µs mechanical FWHM; it just recurs at ~4.2 ms because the carriage free-fall time is repeatable. (This corrects the earlier draft, which read it as a fixed trigger artifact.)
- Sensors were **swapped between positions** and per-event labels weren't posted, so this dataset can't cross-calibrate them. Only events 1 & 4 have both reading a comparable impact; measured in the impact window the single-axis is only **~1.06–1.07×** the tri-axis impact axis on CFC-180 (the two sensors agree within ~5–10 %). The earlier ~1.5× figure was an artifact of taking each channel's *global* CFC-180 maximum — CH1's global peak is a low-frequency post-impact mount oscillation at ~15.8 ms, not the impact. The residual ~250 µs lag and that late oscillation show the sensors are at different mechanical locations, not merely mis-scaled.

## Findings (06/08/2026 co-located calibration series)
- The run **is co-located and time-aligned** (CH1 and CH4 peak within one 8 µs sample at ~4.26 ms across all seven 1000 G drops), so it is finally cross-calibratable.
- **The single-axis reads ~30× the tri-axis.** Zero-intercept fit of the CFC-180 impact-window peaks: **CH1 = 30.8 (±0.3) × CH4**, per-drop ratio **30.8 ± 0.8 (SD)**. For rigidly co-located sensors this is far too large to be a real rigid-body difference — it points to a scale/sensitivity *and* mount-coupling problem, not a real acceleration difference. Both entered sensitivities are internally consistent with their full scales (0.25 mV/G × 20 kG ≈ 5 V; 1.0 mV/G × 10 kG = 10 V), so a simple mV/G typo doesn't obviously explain 30×.
- **CH1 still clips** at +full scale (~20.5 kG) during the impact even with the upgraded 20 kG sensor, then rings to ~−23 kG, while CH4 is a clean ~270 G CFC-180 pulse — so the single-axis mount is far more compliant/resonant (likely the acrylic plate). The 30.8× slope is therefore measured but **not yet a trustworthy correction** until clipping and mount resonance are removed.

## Findings (06/09/2026 corrected-sensitivity, metal-mount series)
- **The ~30× discrepancy is gone — it was the single-axis sensitivity entry.** Re-entering the certificate value (CH1 0.25 → **11.61 mV/G**, a ~46× correction) collapses the gross single-vs-tri factor. The earlier 30.8× was itself a clip-limited *lower bound* on the true ~46× scale error (CH1 was also railing at +20.5 kG on 06/08).
- **Still co-located and time-aligned** — CH1 and CH4 peak at the same ~3.98 ms in all 15 drops, with the off-axis tri-axis channels staying small.
- **But CH1's full scale is now far too *low* (430.7 G)**, because the high 11.61 mV/G sensitivity on a 5 V range gives only 5 V / 11.61 mV/G of range. So CH1 **hard-clips flat at a ~445 G digital rail** for ~300 µs on every 10/15/20 in drop, then rings to ~−500 G, while CH4 (6812 G range) is a clean pulse.
- **The height sweep gives a clean lever arm — on CH4 only.** CH4's CFC-180 impact peak scales repeatably with height (10 in 348.3 ± 2.5 → 15 in 427.1 ± 0.7 → 20 in 498.8 ± 4.0 G) while CH1 stays pinned at the rail. A zero-intercept fit gives CH1 ≈ 0.52 × CH4, but this is **not** a trustworthy factor because CH1 is clipped on every point.

## Findings (06/10/2026 five-channel CH4-vs-CH5 series)
- **The cross-calibration finally closes — and it lands near 1:1.** With a properly-ranged single-axis on CH5 (1.059 mV/G → 9442.9 G range), the zero-intercept fit over all 15 drops is **CH5 = 0.953 (±0.001) × CH4** on the CFC-180 impact window, per-drop ratio **0.952 ± 0.004 (SD)** — repeatable to <0.5 %. Both channels are unclipped and co-located (CH4/CH5 peak within one 8 µs sample), so this is the first **trustworthy** single-vs-tri factor; the residual ~5 % is consistent with the ~1/4 in spacing, not a scale error.
- **Why CH1 still clips is now pinned down: it's the 861 G range, not the mount.** CH1 and CH5 are both single-axis and co-located, so CH5 shows what CH1 *would* read with enough range. The raw transient is ~1500 G (10 in) → ~2800 G (20 in), captured cleanly on CH5 but far above CH1's 861 G full scale (the most its 11.61 mV/G sensitivity allows even on the top 10 V range), so CH1 clips on **14/15** drops while CH5 clips on **0/15**. CH1's clip-limited CH1-vs-CH4 fit (~0.74×, sign even flips between drops) is therefore not usable.

## Recommendations
Step up the single-axis to a higher full-scale (~20,000 G) sensor to stop saturation and verify each sensor's mV/G in TP4; run a back-to-back co-location calibration with repeatable sub-saturation drops (regress CH1 vs CH4 with zero intercept, report slope ± SE); compare CFC-filtered, **impact-windowed** peaks only; address mount resonance; and label sensor/position/orientation per run. Note: the ~4.2 ms CH4 peak is the impact and should be kept, not gated out. For the co-located series specifically: check both sensors' mV/G against their calibration certificates first, mount both on a stiff metal block (not the compliant acrylic plate), keep drops below CH1's full scale, and sweep the impact amplitude so the regression has a real lever arm. For the corrected-sensitivity 06/09 series: the sensitivity fix solved the original disagreement, so the only remaining blocker is the CH1 input range — raise CH1's voltage range (full scale ≥ ~1000 G for these 10–20 in drops) so it stops clipping, then redo the CFC-filtered, impact-windowed, zero-intercept CH1-vs-CH4 regression over the existing height sweep; with both unclipped and co-located on the metal load it should land near 1:1. The 06/10 five-channel series confirms this: the properly-ranged CH5 single-axis lands at 0.953 (±0.001) × CH4, so going forward **use CH5 (the 1.059 mV/G single-axis) as the working single-axis** — its 9442.9 G range covers the raw drop-tower transient, whereas the 11.61 mV/G CH1 unit is intrinsically mis-ranged (861 G full scale can't be raised further, since 10 V is already the top range) and should be reserved for sub-~800 G work only.

> Note: the channel→sensor mapping is inferred from the data. The "both sensors on the bottom acrylic plate" assumption applies only to the 06/08 series; @ctrhjk later clarified that the 06/09 and 06/10 series had the acrylic plates removed with both sensors on the bare metal load (CH1/CH2–CH4 unmoved between 06/09 and 06/10, with CH5 added on the very left).

Adds a submission-ready abstract for the TMS 2027 Annual Meeting & Exhibition, derived from the project's existing tensegrity energy-absorption work and kept consistent with `idetc-abstract.tex`.

### Added — `tms-2027-abstract.md`
- **Submission metadata** — TMS 2027 (Orlando, Mar 14–18, 2027), abstract deadline Jul 1, 2026, plain-text ≤150-word format, oral preference.
- **Target symposium** — *AI-Enabled Materials Processing: Integrating Accelerated Experimental Workflows and Processing-Aware Machine Learning* (covers Bayesian optimization, surrogate models, closed-loop experimental workflows).
- **Title / authors** — *Closed-Loop Bayesian Optimization of Multi-Material 3D-Printed Tensegrity-Inspired Energy Absorbers*; full tensegrity team in first-paper author order: Marcus Madsen\*, Audrey Christiansen\*, Jinkwan Han\*, Jeffrey R. Hill† (presenting), Sterling G. Baird† (all Department of Mechanical Engineering, BYU), with \* and † equal-contribution footnotes.
- **Abstract body** — 141-word plain-text summary of the multi-material FDM (PLA + TPU) design–print–test loop driven by multi-objective BO on measured force/SEA/efficiency.

### Added — Edison symposium-fit feedback (`edison-trajectories/tms-symposium-fit/` + `scripts/edison/`)
- Submitted an Edison ANALYSIS task (`16895002`) with the abstract and the symposium call-for-abstracts flyer attached, asking how well the abstract fits the current symposium and whether an additive-manufacturing-focused symposium would fit better. Committed the fetched answer, full task dump, README headline, and reusable `submit_tms_symposium_fit.py` / `fetch_tms_symposium_fit.py` driver scripts.
- **Headline:** as written the abstract is a weak fit (~4/10) for the current symposium #021 (which wants processing as a primary design variable). Best as-written home is AM-track symposium #003 *"Additive Manufacturing Modeling, Simulation, and AI: Microstructure, Mechanics, and Process"* (~8.5/10, minimal edits). To credibly keep #021 (~7/10), add FDM process variables (interface overlap, PLA/TPU nozzle temperature, layer height, print speed) plus a process-sensitive response to the BO loop. Backups: #023 and #005.

### Notes for review
- Word count verified at 141 (TMS limit 150).
- Presenting author, oral-vs-poster preference, and symposium choice are easy to adjust before submission.
- The abstract is left unchanged pending a team decision between moving to AM symposium #003 (as-written) or adding print-parameter optimization to stay in #021; ready-to-paste rewrites for both paths are included in the Edison answer.

body:
The issue asked who to contact at BYU for permission to drop a scaled-up tensegrity from the Kimball Tower, and what "CMR" stands for (and its role in producing a video). This adds a reference note answering both.

New file: `reviews/byu-kimball-tower-drop-outreach.md`.

### Contents
- **Building** — identifies the Kimball Tower as the Spencer W. Kimball Tower (KMBL/SWKT), the occupied 12-story / ~161 ft tallest campus building, so a drop is treated as a high-risk/special-use activity routed through multiple offices.
- **Contacts (ordered)** — PI Jeff Hill → Risk Management & Safety (gatekeeper) → Physical Facilities Building Operations → KMBL tenant colleges → University Communications → Fulton College engineering, with verify-first phone numbers and links.
- **"CMR"** — Compliant Mechanisms Research group (Mech. Eng., Larry Howell), known for student-produced engineering video; engage via an internal intro from Hill. Flags University Communications as the alternative if a media office was meant.
- **Likely permit conditions** — exclusion/landing zone, spotters, tethered/recoverable specimen, insurance, off-peak scheduling, on-site responsible faculty.

### Open questions for reviewers
- Confirm "CMR" = Compliant Mechanisms Research group vs. a campus media office.
- Confirm the Kimball Tower (occupied tower) is still the intended drop site vs. an engineering building or the existing bungee drop tower, which would be far easier to permit.

Contacts/numbers are sourced from public BYU pages and carry a verify-before-acting caveat; they should be confirmed directly.
title: Document BYU outreach path for Kimball Tower tensegrity drop test and clarify "CMR"
